en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Youth King Golden Light,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Dharma Xian, Imperial Subject and Grand Master of Enlightened Teaching,
who served as Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial during the Chao-san Dafu period, by imperial decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Grove Monastery in the city of Kapilavastu.

At that time, there was a youth among the Śākya clan named King Golden Light (*Suvarṇaprabhāsa*). His physical appearance was dignified and majestic, his limbs were perfectly proportioned, and his radiance was as brilliant as the sun and moon. He was exceptionally intelligent, surpassing others in his sharp wit; he possessed natural respectfulness and diligence without needing external encouragement. He disciplined his mind through the guidance of teachers and elders, and he was endowed with all manner of rare jewels and precious playthings.

Although he constantly enjoyed these things, he was free from greedy attachment; together with his own retinue of fifteen hundred concubines and female musicians, he always dwelt within the palace, experiencing its pleasures.
At that time, one day, the youth suddenly heard people say:

"In the past, the World-Honored One, seeing the suffering and affliction of saṃsāra within the three realms, renounced the rank of a wheel-turning monarch, left the home life to practice austerities, perfected the Buddha-way, sat beneath a tree to subdue the four kinds of Māras, and realized unsurpassed awakening."
Upon hearing this, the youth was filled with great joy; he immediately took his kinsmen and attendants, surrounding him on all sides, and proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.

Approaching the gate of the vihāra, he cast aside his pride and advanced on foot with his retinue. Having reached the presence of the Buddha, he joined his palms in reverence, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and praised him, saying:

"The body of the Tathāgata is like a mountain of gold, and like a jeweled banner adorned with every kind of treasure. His face is like the full moon, pure and radiant, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics. His light shines afar, like a thousand suns."

Noble, auspicious, and of great wisdom and diligence, endowed with vast merit and possessing both fortune and insight, you know all phenomena and have severed all doubts. Possessing omniscience, you are the teacher of gods and humans; the father of the three realms, you rescue all sentient beings, appearing in the world so that all who see you rejoice.

At that time, having offered this praise, the youth circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side, desiring to hear the sublime Dharma. He further gave rise to this thought:
"I was born in a royal palace with such merit and reward, and possess great power and influence; what are the causes and conditions for this?"

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the youth Suvarṇaprabhāsa as well as the aspiration of the assembled multitude to hear the Dharma, extensively expounded for them the twelve links of dependent origination and the four noble truths.

Excellent in the beginning, middle, and end; its phrasing is skillful, its meaning profound and far-reaching, pure and unadulterated, and it is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy life of Brahma-faring.
Having expounded this Dharma, he further spoke of the causes, conditions, retributions, and responses regarding the past life of the youth Suvarṇaprabhāsa.
He said to the youth:

"In the distant past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata Vipaśyin—Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—who taught the Dharma to transform and edify sentient beings, bringing them benefit and joy. Having completed his buddha-work, he then entered parinirvāṇa."

"At that time, there was a man whose occupation was farming; although he labored diligently, he was always lacking. Nevertheless, he delighted in practicing various virtues and, by reducing his own bodily and verbal comforts and diminishing his accumulated wealth, he fashioned an image of Vipaśyin to offer as worship. I shall now describe the karmic fruit he obtained."

"O Bhikṣus! The merit obtained by that person who engaged in agriculture will cause him to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King over the four continents for hundreds of thousands of births; he shall fly through the air, be endowed with the seven treasures, attain great sovereign power, emit radiance from his body, and experience the most supreme bliss in birth after birth."
Having received this merit, he was further born among the gods of the six heavens of the desire realm as their lord, experiencing great happiness for hundreds of thousands of lifetimes;

for another hundred thousand lifetimes he was the Brahmā King, for a hundred thousand lifetimes he was the Lord of Pure Light, and for a hundred thousand lifetimes he was the lord of the four formless realms.

Having experienced such sublime celestial pleasures at that time, they later descend to the human realm to be born into the kṣatriya, brāhmaṇa, or vaiśya castes, where they constantly occupy royal thrones and attain great sovereignty.

“O Bhikṣus! This youth has come from the celestial realm and was born into a royal palace; having previously performed meritorious deeds, he cannot be harmed or diminished, nor shall he fall away, but will later attain the outflow-free state and realize nirvāṇa.”
“O Bhikṣus! That person who fashioned the image was none other than the youth Suvarṇaprabha.
I have already explained all the causes and effects thereof.”
Furthermore, there are those who, using crystal, or mani-jewels, or gold, or silver, or brass, or copper, or even wood, stone, or ivory, cast, mold, carve, or engrave images of the Buddha;
whether they contain relics or not, whether they are short or long, large or small, or even images made from scented clay—such are the karmic fruits of creating images.

“O Bhikṣus! If there are sons or daughters of good family who, with a pure and sincere mind, bathe any one of the images they have fashioned according to the Dharma using exquisite scented water, I shall now describe the merit they obtain.”

These sons and daughters of good family, as they cast off one body and receive another, will always be born into noble lineages such as the Kṣatriya, Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, or Śūdra; their merit will be perfected, they will be endowed with the marks of a great man, they will attain the knowledge of past lives, and they will obtain virtuous kinsmen.
As for servants, slaves, carriages, horses, rare jewels, and wealth, there is nothing among all their enjoyments that is not fully provided;

they serve as a refuge and a leader for all sentient beings, and those who see them rejoice, speaking with full compliance. They are constantly remembered by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats, and whatever they wish or seek, they obtain it all.
"O Bhikṣus! Even a mass of merit such as this cannot be fully illustrated by analogy, let alone the merit of creating an image.
As for all afflictions—such as jealousy, hatred, attachment, greed, anger, and delusion—one will swiftly attain liberation from them, and by practicing gradually, realize unsurpassed enlightenment."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"After my parinirvāṇa, if there are men or women who fashion images from various jewels and bathe them with exquisite scented water,"
Furthermore, by offering delightful flowers with a sincere mind, one will,
in future lives, obtain the retribution of a handsome and dignified form;
all sentient beings will gaze upon them without ever being satiated.
One obtains various karmic fruits: nobility and happiness.
By means of these remaining wholesome deeds, one becomes far removed from all afflictions;
the clouds and veils of delusive darkness are dispelled, like the moon dwelling in the void.
Thereafter, further sustained by superior power, he was reborn in the celestial realms;
becoming a sovereign of the gods, he enjoyed happiness for a hundred kalpas.
When his lifespan there came to an end, he descended to be born as a Wheel-Turning King.
His physical form is like that of a celestial being, And his merit is most preeminent;
The seven treasures constantly follow him, And he possesses supernatural powers and mastery.
He travels throughout the realms of the four continents, Attaining everything according to his will.
Later they enter the Noble Path, and eventually realize Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who encounter a Buddha stūpa containing śarīra relics as minute as fine dust.
If this person’s heart is filled with joy and they perform various kinds of offerings,
they shall obtain a great mass of merit, no different from what was mentioned before.
The transformation body of the Tathāgata pervades the triple world.
The merit of this person’s offerings and the various karmic fruits they induce—
even their renown— pervade the ten directions.
Their physical form is like pure gold, and their radiance shines eternally and brilliantly.
"In the heavens and among humans, you shall experience immeasurable happiness.

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s extensive exposition of the subtle and wondrous Dharma, as well as the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions of the past, the youth Suvarṇaprabhāsa felt no attachment in his heart toward his kinsmen. Disgusted with and weary of wealth and honor, he renounced pleasure and sought to leave the household life within the True Dharma.
The Buddha immediately ordained him as a śramaṇa at that very moment, and he soon realized the fruit of arhatship; his retinue, likewise, all realized the fruits of the path while seated there.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the youth Suvarṇaprabhāsa, together with his retinue and the assembly gathered there, received it with joy and faith, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew.
Thus ends the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-kumāra-sūtra*.
